summary: Updates the Sieve filtering language with an extension for variables. Scripts can store data, use stored values in strings, and test the content of a string. This lets rules keep state across rules. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Variables are labeled boxes where a mail rule can save something and use it later.

questions: how to set variables in sieve
what is the sieve variables extension
how do i set a variable in sieve
how do i test a string in sieve
subtitle: Gives Sieve mail filters named variables, string substitution and a way to test the result.

tldr.problem: Larger Sieve rule sets need to keep state or configuration details across rules, but the base language has no way to store a value and use it later.
tldr.mechanism: The extension makes strings expand ${name} references, adds a set action that stores values (with optional modifiers), adds a string test, and exposes wildcard matches as numbered match variables.
tldr.outcome: Scripts that require the variables capability can build file names, reuse values and examine strings. RFC 5229 updates RFC 5228 and is itself updated by RFC 5173.

today: RFC 5229 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5228 and is itself updated by RFC 5173. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the Variables Extension Adds
sections.content:
RFC 5229 is an extension to the Sieve email filtering language defined in RFC 5228. It adds support for storing and referencing named data. In advanced rule sets it is useful to keep state or configuration details across rules, and this is how Sieve gets that ability.

The extension only applies to scripts that include a require clause for the capability string variables. The require clauses themselves are not affected. Three things change: how strings are interpreted, a new set action stores data, and a new string test examines a string's value.
sections.eli5: Normally a mail rule forgets everything between steps. This add-on gives it a notebook so it can remember things.

sections.title: How Strings Expand Variables
sections.content:
Once the extension is enabled, quoted strings and multi-line literals can contain references of the form ${name}. When a string is evaluated, each reference is replaced by the value of that variable. Only one pass through the string is made, variable names are case insensitive (so foo and FOO are the same variable), and unknown variables become the empty string. A string that holds no substitutions is a constant string.

Text that is not a valid reference is left alone. With company set to ACME, the string ${BAD${Company} becomes ${BADACME, and ${doh!} stays unchanged because ! is not legal in an identifier. The expanded string uses the variable values current when control reaches the statement.

Backslash quoting and encoded-character processing are both resolved before variable substitution. To include a literal ${beep}, store a dollar sign in a variable (set "dollar" "$") and write ${dollar}{beep}.

A reference may start with a namespace such as name.. Namespaces are reserved for future extensions that expose internal state, which SHOULD use a namespace matching their capability string. Referring to a namespace without a prior require for its extension MUST cause an error.
sections.eli5: If you write a name inside a special wrapper, the filter swaps it for whatever is in that box, like filling in a name on a form letter. If the box is empty, you get nothing.

sections.title: Match Variables
sections.content:
A match variable has a name made only of decimal digits and no namespace. It refers to the list of strings from the most recent successful :matches test. Index 0 holds the matched part of the source value, and index 1 onward holds what each wildcard (the question mark and the asterisk) matched, in order, possibly as an empty string. Wildcards match as little as possible. If the index is out of range, the empty string is substituted, and the list is empty if no match has succeeded.

For example, matching the List-ID header against a pattern with three asterisks lets a script file mail with fileinto "INBOX.lists.${2}". Tests are short-circuited and evaluated left to right, so in anyof (true, ...) the second test never runs and no match variables are set.

A new match type, such as a regular-expression one, MAY specify that it also sets match variables when the variables extension is enabled.
sections.eli5: When a pattern with wildcard blanks matches an email, the filter remembers what filled each blank, so it can say what was in the first blank, the second, and so on.

sections.title: The set Action and Its Modifiers
sections.content:
The set action has the form set [MODIFIER] <name: string> <value: string>. The name MUST be a constant string and a valid variable name; an invalid name MUST be detected as a syntax error. Match variables cannot be set, and a namespace cannot be used unless an extension explicitly allows it. Variables are visible only to the currently running script. The action does not affect the implicit keep and is compatible with all actions in RFC 5228.

Modifiers change the value before it is stored. They are :lower, :upper, :lowerfirst, :upperfirst, :quotewildcard and :length. Unknown modifiers MUST yield a syntax error. When several are given they apply from highest precedence to lowest, and two modifiers of the same precedence in one set is an error.

  • :length stores the decimal count of characters in the expansion.
  • :quotewildcard prefixes the asterisk, the question mark and the backslash with a backslash, so the text matches only literally in :matches.
  • The case modifiers only change US-ASCII letters A to Z and a to z.

For instance, set :upperfirst :lower "b" "${a}" with a holding juMBlEd lETteRS stores Jumbled letters.
sections.eli5: Setting a variable is writing in a box. You can also ask the filter to tidy the words first, like making them all capitals, or to write down just how many letters there are.

sections.title: The string Test
sections.content:
The string test has the form string [MATCH-TYPE] [COMPARATOR] <source: string-list> <key-list: string-list>. It is true if any source string matches any key, and the match type defaults to :is.

Unlike the header and address tests, both the source and the keys come from the script, not from the message. Whitespace stripping MUST NOT be done unless the script explicitly requests it through some future mechanism. This lets a script examine a variable it built earlier.

With the relational extension, the :count match type counts a single string as 0 if it is empty and 1 otherwise. A string list's count is the sum of its members' counts.
sections.eli5: The string test asks a yes or no question about words the script already has, like checking whether your sticky note says what you think it says.

sections.title: Implementation Limits
sections.content:
An implementation MUST support at least 128 distinct variables, variable names of at least 32 characters, and values of at least 4000 characters. If a script tries to store more than the implementation supports, this SHOULD be reported as an error at compile time when possible. If it is found at run time, the value SHOULD be truncated, and this MUST NOT be treated as an error.

Match variables ${1} through ${9} MUST be supported. A reference to a higher index than the implementation supports MUST be treated as a syntax error, which SHOULD be discovered at compile time.
sections.eli5: Every filter has to have at least a certain number of boxes, and each box has to hold at least a certain amount of writing. If you write too much, the extra is cut off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With match variables, a careless script author can end up with strings that hold arbitrary values controlled by the sender of the mail. Because values over the implementation limit are silently truncated, large structures with security implications should not be stored in variables.

Variables make advanced decisions easier to write, but there is no looping construct, so all Sieve scripts terminate in an orderly manner. The RFC also warns that Sieve should not be relied on as a security measure against hostile mail. It is designed for simple, mostly static tests and is not suitable as a spam or virus checker, where the sender has a motive to vary the mail's format.
sections.eli5: Anyone can send you mail, so be careful what you copy from it into your boxes. And this filter is a sorting helper, not a guard that stops bad mail.
